pages.name: The Gift and the Three Moons

text.content:
Compiled for the instruction of apprentices by the archivists of Wayreth, and revised in the year 351 by order of the Master.

Magic is not an achievement. It is a loan.

Every mage on Krynn is taught this before they are taught anything useful, and most of them spend the rest of their lives resenting it. The power a wizard draws does not originate in the wizard. It is given by the three gods of magic, and what is given may be withdrawn.

The three are siblings, and like most siblings they agree on precisely one thing.

  • Solinari, the silver moon, son of Paladine and Mishakal. He gives his power to those who would use magic to protect and to build. His followers wear white.
  • Lunitari, the red moon, daughter of Gilean. She gives her power to those who serve magic itself, taking no side but the art's. Her followers wear red.
  • Nuitari, the black moon, son of Takhisis and Sargonnas. He gives his power to those who would use magic to rule. His followers wear black. He is invisible to all but those who serve him, which tells you most of what you need to know about him.

The one thing they agree on is this: magic must not be lost. Whatever the three gods think of each other — and they have gone to war over it — they have never once permitted the art to die. When the Kingpriest came for the wizards, the three moons did not save their followers. They saved the magic. There is a difference, and every apprentice learns it eventually.

The Moons and Power

The moons wax and wane on cycles that do not match, and a wizard's strength moves with their god's moon. A Black Robe on the night of high sanction is a different creature than the same mage a week later. This is not metaphor. It is arithmetic, and it is why Conclave business is scheduled the way it is.

Once every five hundred and four days all three moons come full together. The Night of the Eye. Every mage on Krynn feels it, whether they understand what they are feeling or not.

DM Note — Moon Mechanics

Full mechanical treatment is in Moons and Sanction. If you want the short version: a wizard of a given Order gains a scaling benefit during their moon's high sanction and takes a penalty during its low. It is worth tracking, because it turns "when do we attack the Tower" into a real question with a real answer.

pages.name: The Founding of the Five Towers

text.content:
In the years after the Graygem, magic on Krynn was a scattered and dangerous thing. Hedge-wizards, sorcerers who had bargained with things better left alone, self-taught practitioners who blew themselves and their villages apart learning the difference between a fire spell and a mistake. There was no order to it. There was no accountability. There was, very quickly, a great deal of fear.

The gods of magic did what gods do when their followers embarrass them. They intervened.

The three Orders were established: White, Red, and Black, each bound to a moon, all three bound to one another by an oath that has never been formally broken and has been informally violated approximately once a decade ever since. The Conclave was formed to govern them. And five Towers of High Sorcery were raised to house the Orders, to train the gifted, and — the part that is rarely said aloud — to make magic visible, so that kings knew exactly where to send their complaints.

The Five

  • Wayreth, raised first, in the deep south, wrapped in a forest that was old before the Tower was new. Seat of the Conclave.
  • Palanthas, raised in the great northern city, beautiful and public and proud.
  • Daltigoth, in the Ergothian west.
  • Losarcum, in the stone deserts of the south, cut into the rock.
  • Istar, in the golden city, in the shadow of a temple that would eventually decide it did not care for neighbours.

Five Towers. For most of recorded history, five. The number is worth sitting with, because a student who grows up hearing "the Towers of High Sorcery" and then walks into the only one left standing tends to feel the arithmetic personally.

What a Tower Was For

A Tower was never only a school. It was a vault for artifacts too dangerous to leave in the world, a court where the Conclave tried its own, a laboratory, a library, and a fortress. The Towers were built to be defensible against armies, which struck contemporaries as paranoid and turned out to be optimistic.

pages.name: The Age of Might and the Kingpriest

text.content:
The Kingpriest of Istar did not begin by hating wizards. He began by loving good, which is more dangerous.

Istar rose over centuries into the greatest power Ansalon had known, and its church rose with it, and somewhere in that rise the idea took hold that evil was not a condition of the soul but a stain on the world — something that could be identified, isolated, and removed. It is a very appealing idea. It is also the beginning of every atrocity in recorded history.

The wizards were an obvious target, and not an unfair one. The Orders included Black Robes. The Conclave openly seated practitioners who served the daughter of Takhisis and made no apology for it. When the church demanded to know how an institution could claim neutrality while sheltering evil, the Conclave's answer — that magic belongs to no alignment and that the balance requires all three — was philosophically sound and politically suicidal.

They asked us to expel the Black Robes. We told them the truth: that we could not, that the god of the black moon would simply raise his own Order outside our walls and beyond our reach, and that a Nuitari unwatched is a Nuitari unbound. They heard only that we would not.

— attributed to the Conclave's last embassy to Istar

The Edicts

The persecution came in stages, as these things do. First the Edict of Thought Control, which made unsanctioned magic a crime. Then the licensing, the registries, the requirement that wizards declare themselves. Then the mobs, which the church did not organise and did not discourage.

By the end, a robed mage could not walk in Istar, Daltigoth, or Losarcum without an escort. The Towers stood, but they stood like islands in a rising sea.

The wizards fought back. This is the part of the history the Conclave records plainly and without pride.

The conflict that followed is remembered as the Lost Battles, a name that admits the outcome in advance. It was not a war between armies. It was a war between an institution of a few thousand practitioners and an empire with the enthusiastic backing of half a continent, and it went exactly as that description suggests.

The Orders won engagements. Wizards are extremely good at winning engagements. They lost the war, because there is no spell for being outnumbered by a hundred to one indefinitely, and because every victory confirmed to the world that the church had been right about them all along.

The Bargain

When it became clear the Towers would fall, the Conclave made a decision that has defined the Orders ever since. They negotiated.

The terms: the wizards would surrender the Towers of Daltigoth, Istar, and Losarcum. In exchange, the Orders would be permitted to withdraw — alive — to Wayreth, and Palanthas would remain in their hands.

The Kingpriest accepted. He got three Towers and the humiliation of the Conclave, and he judged that sufficient. He was wrong about that too, but that comes later.

DM Note — Why This Matters at Your Table

The Lost Battles are the load-bearing trauma of the entire institution. Every Conclave decision in 351 AC is made by people whose predecessors surrendered three Towers to avoid extinction and have spent three centuries arguing about whether that was cowardice or wisdom.

This is the argument Raistlin wins. Hold onto it — it comes back in The Concession of Wayreth.

Three Towers were surrendered. Only one of them was ever occupied.

Daltigoth and Losarcum

The wizards of Daltigoth and Losarcum destroyed their Towers rather than hand them over intact. Not out of spite — or not only out of spite. A Tower of High Sorcery is a vault, and the things in the vaults could not be permitted to fall into the hands of an institution that believed it was incapable of error.

Losarcum's destruction took a substantial portion of the city with it. The stone quarter came down. Whether that was intended is a question the Conclave has never answered in writing, and the archivists who might have known are three centuries dead.

Istar

The Tower of Istar was surrendered whole. The Kingpriest took possession, found the vaults empty and the libraries stripped, and converted the building into a monument to his own victory. It stood for a handful of years, and then the mountain fell on it along with everything else in the city, and the Conclave has never once been heard to express regret about this.

Palanthas

Palanthas is the one that matters, and it deserves its own page.

Under the terms of the bargain, the Tower of Palanthas remained in the Conclave's hands. That was the agreement. It lasted until the Kingpriest's influence reached Palanthas's Lord and the Conclave was informed, politely, that the city would prefer the wizards to leave.

The Orders agreed to withdraw. The evacuation was orderly. The Master of the Tower had the keys ready to hand over. And then a young Red Robe — whose name the Conclave's official record preserves and whose reasons it does not — climbed to the highest window and threw himself from it onto the gate below.

He was still alive when he hit. He had time for one sentence.

The gates shall remain closed and the halls empty until the day comes when the master of both past and present returns with power.

Then he died, impaled on the spikes of the gate, and the Tower of Palanthas closed itself.

What the Curse Did

Nothing subtle. The Tower became a wound in the city. The grove around it — the Shoikan Grove — grew in a single night into something that is not, in any meaningful sense, a forest. Every soul who has attempted entry since has died, gone mad, or come out changed in ways that make the other two look preferable.

Palanthas, a city that prides itself on beauty, has spent three hundred years arranging its architecture so that people do not have to look at it.

DM Note — The Prophecy

"The master of both past and present" is the hook, and in a campaign where Raistlin holds Wayreth it becomes urgent rather than ominous. Raistlin is a Black Robe who has already taken one Tower by an unprecedented route. The Conclave is aware that the phrasing fits him unnervingly well and that he is aware of it too.

Suggested use: the party is not sent to Palanthas. The party is sent to find out whether Raistlin intends to go there, which is a much better mission because they cannot solve it by killing anything.

Five Towers. Two destroyed, one buried under the Cataclysm, one cursed shut. One left.

Wayreth is the last Tower of High Sorcery on Krynn, and it has been for three hundred years. Every Conclave is held there. Every Test is administered there. Every artifact the Orders reclaimed from the surrendered vaults is stored there. If Wayreth falls, the institution of High Sorcery does not relocate. It ends.

The Conclave understands this. It is why they are cautious to the point of paralysis, why they hoard, why they have not meaningfully intervened in a war being fought four hundred miles to the north, and why an unusually persuasive Black Robe was able to make an argument they could not answer.

The Forest

Wayreth cannot be found by looking for it. The forest that surrounds the Tower moves — not the trees individually, though there are accounts of that too, but the forest as a fact. Travellers who set out for Wayreth arrive at empty moorland. Travellers who set out for somewhere else entirely find themselves walking under trees they do not recognise, on a path they did not choose, toward a Tower they were not looking for.

The standard explanation is that the Tower is warded, that the forest is an extension of those wards, and that the Conclave controls who arrives. The standard explanation is incomplete.

DM Note — The Forest Decides

The Conclave does not control the Forest of Wayreth. It never has. The forest admits whom it chooses, and the Conclave has spent three centuries constructing an institutional fiction that its own admissions policy is doing the work.

This is the secret that pays off the entire premise. Par-Salian did not step down because Raistlin out-argued him. He stepped down because the forest stopped letting him in, and he understood immediately what that meant.

Do not reveal this early. Let the players believe the political version — it is a good version. The reveal lands hardest when a PC is standing in the forest and realises the path is not taking them where the Conclave said it would.

The Three Orders

Robe colour is not a costume and it is not, strictly, an alignment. It is a declaration of what you believe magic is for, and the god of that moon either accepts the declaration or does not.

  • White Robes. Magic as a shield. Restrained, institutional, and rather more comfortable with rules than any of the others. They tend to hold the Conclave's administrative offices, largely because the other two Orders find the work tedious.
  • Red Robes. Magic as an end in itself. Loyal to the art before any cause, which their siblings variously describe as principled or as an elaborate excuse for doing whatever they like.
  • Black Robes. Magic as a means. Ambitious, disciplined, and considerably better organised than outsiders expect — Nuitari does not tolerate sloppiness in his servants, and a Black Robe who is careless does not remain a Black Robe long.

All three take the same Test. All three sit the same Conclave. A White Robe and a Black Robe who would happily kill each other in the field will vote in the same chamber, because the alternative — three separate institutions, three separate agendas, no oversight at all — is a thing every one of them has been taught to fear since apprenticeship.

Structure

Twenty-one seats. Seven per Order. The Head of the Conclave is drawn from whichever Order the moons favour, though in practice the office has been held by a White Robe for most of living memory, and the Master of the Tower of Wayreth has customarily been the same person.

Customarily. In 351 AC, those two offices are held by different people for the first time in three centuries, and the Conclave has not finished deciding how it feels about that.

DM Note — The Split

This is your political engine. Par-Salian remains Head of the Conclave. Raistlin is Master of the Tower. The Head convenes the Orders; the Master controls the building they must convene in, the vaults, the wards, and the Tests.

Neither can act without the other. Both know it. Every scene set in Wayreth should have this tension running underneath it.

Renegades

A wizard who takes the Test and passes is a Wizard of High Sorcery. A wizard who refuses the Test, or takes it and flees, is a renegade, and the Conclave hunts them.

Not as a formality. Renegade hunters are dispatched, they are competent, and they are authorised to use lethal force at their discretion. The Orders' position is that unaccountable magic is what produced the Lost Battles and that they will not permit it a second time. The renegades' position is that this is an institution demanding submission at swordpoint and calling it stewardship.

Both positions are correct. That is rather the problem.
